description: Table 4 is a five-column, four-row rendered data table (no axes, no micrograph, no scale bar) reporting room-temperature Vickers microhardness of Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5) low-density as-rolled steels. Column headers, printed exactly, are: "Samples", "Matrix (austenite) hardness (HV)", "Error", "Ferrite hardness (HV)", "Error". Row values: 0Be → 415.55 ±12.481 matrix, ferrite "−"; 0.5Be → 470.97 ±20.241 matrix, ferrite "−"; 1.0Be → 398.39 ±14.630 matrix and 349.81 ±21.267 ferrite; 1.5Be → 407.01 ±17.551 matrix and 371.50 ±23.002 ferrite. The dashes indicate that no ferrite hardness was measured for 0Be and 0.5Be, consistent with those being single-phase austenitic steels while 1.0Be and 1.5Be are dual-phase austenite (γ) + ferrite (δ). In every sample where both are given, ferrite is softer than the austenitic matrix. The table's claim is that Be addition raises austenite hardness up to 0.5Be (peak 470.97 HV) but that at 1.0Be and 1.5Be the appearance of softer ferrite lowers the average matrix hardness while the ferrite itself hardens slightly from 1.0Be to 1.5Be.

subfigures.description: Single rendered table (Table 4) with columns Samples / Matrix (austenite) hardness (HV) / Error / Ferrite hardness (HV) / Error, and rows 0Be, 0.5Be, 1.0Be, 1.5Be. Matrix hardness: 415.55 ±12.481, 470.97 ±20.241, 398.39 ±14.630, 407.01 ±17.551 HV. Ferrite hardness only for 1.0Be (349.81 ±21.267) and 1.5Be (371.50 ±23.002); 0Be and 0.5Be show dashes.

observations.observation: The table has five columns: Samples, Matrix (austenite) hardness (HV), Error, Ferrite hardness (HV), Error — the matrix column is explicitly assigned to austenite.
Matrix (austenite) hardness of the 0Be as-rolled steel is 415.55 HV with error ±12.481.
Matrix (austenite) hardness of 0.5Be is 470.97 HV (±20.241), the highest matrix value in the table, exceeding 0Be by a clear margin.
Matrix (austenite) hardness of 1.0Be is 398.39 HV (±14.630) and of 1.5Be is 407.01 HV (±17.551), i.e. both lower than 0Be and 0.5Be.
Ferrite hardness is reported only for 1.0Be (349.81 ±21.267) and 1.5Be (371.50 ±23.002); the 0Be and 0.5Be ferrite cells contain a dash, meaning not measured/not applicable.
For both dual-phase samples the ferrite hardness is lower than the corresponding matrix (austenite) hardness (349.81 vs 398.39 HV; 371.50 vs 407.01 HV).
The table caption states it reports microhardness of Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe low-density as-rolled steels.
The citing text states microhardness was measured with an FM-ARS9000 Vickers hardness tester.

The citing text states that 0Be and 0.5Be steels are austenitic whereas 1.0Be and 1.5Be steels are dual-phase austenite (γ) + ferrite (δ), which matches the appearance of ferrite columns only for the latter two.

The citing text asserts that in austenitic steels hardness increases significantly with increasing Be content, whereas in the table the austenite hardness rises from 0Be to 0.5Be but falls for 1.0Be (398.39 HV) and 1.5Be (407.01 HV); the figure therefore only partially confirms this statement.

The citing text states the hardness of 1.5Be steel is 9 HV higher than that of 1.0Be steel; the table's matrix values differ by 8.62 HV (407.01 vs 398.39) and its ferrite values by 21.69 HV (371.50 vs 349.81).
The citing text attributes the lower average matrix hardness of the dual-phase steels to their high ferrite content, consistent with softer ferrite values in the table.
